topic.subject: physics
topic.title: Colour, vision and the eye
topic.scopeBasis: TGS 2025-26: Light and the Eye; TGS 2026-27: Waves 2
topic.overview: White light contains a spectrum of colours. What we see depends on which wavelengths reach the eye and how the eye focuses and detects them.
learningGoals: Recall the precise Year 8 scientific vocabulary and symbols.
Apply the idea to an unfamiliar example rather than relying on recognition.
Use the command word, show working where needed and include every mark point.
mustMemoriseRules: White light can be dispersed into the visible spectrum: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet.
An opaque object's colour depends mainly on the light it reflects; other incident colours are absorbed.
A coloured filter transmits a limited range of colours and absorbs most others.
Red, green and blue are the primary colours of light; combining all three at suitable intensities produces white light.
Light is refracted by the cornea and lens and focused on the retina.
The iris changes pupil size to control light entering the eye; it does not focus the image.
Rods are very sensitive in dim light; cones provide colour vision and fine detail in brighter light.
The optic nerve carries electrical impulses from the retina to the brain.

mustMemoriseVocabulary.meaning: the range of component colours in visible light
separation of white light into colours by refraction
take in light energy rather than transmit or reflect it
a material that transmits selected wavelengths and absorbs others
transparent curved front of the eye that refracts light
coloured ring of muscle controlling pupil size
light-sensitive layer containing rods and cones
nerve carrying impulses from retina to brain

workedExamples.prompt: A red apple is lit only by blue light. Predict its appearance.
workedExamples.answer: Very dark or black because it normally reflects red light but little blue light is available to reflect.

workedExamples.prompt: What does a red filter do to white light?
workedExamples.answer: It mainly transmits red wavelengths and absorbs most other visible wavelengths.

practicals.title: Colour and filters
practicals.aim: Investigate how filters change the light reflected from coloured objects.
practicals.variables: IV: filter or incident-light colour; DV: observed brightness/colour; controls: object, lamp distance and room lighting.
practicals.method: View the same coloured objects under white light and then through different filters or under coloured light; record observations systematically.
practicals.expectedResult: Objects appear bright only when the incident light contains colours they can reflect and the viewing filter transmits them.
practicals.safety: Do not stare into bright lamps or lasers; use cool, teacher-approved sources.
practicals.evaluation: Darken the room consistently, repeat observations and distinguish subjective colour names from measured intensity.

commonMistakes: Saying objects contain coloured light of their own.
Saying a filter adds its colour to incoming light.
Saying the pupil focuses light onto the retina.
examTips: Trace the journey: source -> object/filter -> eye.
Ask which colours are available, reflected and transmitted.
For eye questions, give each structure one precise job.
beforeStartingPractice: Read the key rules once, cover them, then retrieve them aloud or in writing.
Use MC first for confidence, but finish with typed, calculation, practical or explanation evidence.
After an error, study the explanation; the same concept returns later in a different format and again after 2 and 7 days.

practicals.subject: physics
practicals.title: Colour and filters
practicals.aim: Investigate how filters change the light reflected from coloured objects.
practicals.variables: IV: filter or incident-light colour; DV: observed brightness/colour; controls: object, lamp distance and room lighting.
practicals.method: View the same coloured objects under white light and then through different filters or under coloured light; record observations systematically.
practicals.expectedResult: Objects appear bright only when the incident light contains colours they can reflect and the viewing filter transmits them.
practicals.safety: Do not stare into bright lamps or lasers; use cool, teacher-approved sources.
practicals.evaluation: Darken the room consistently, repeat observations and distinguish subjective colour names from measured intensity.
